online-safety-for-children-a-parents-gui:
Online risk is usually discussed as one thing. It is four, they need different responses, and confusing them is why so much online safety advice feels simultaneously alarming and useless.

The four

Content. What a child might see: violence, pornography, self-harm material, extremist content, or an algorithm that has decided what they should watch next. The response here is design. Filters, restricted modes, autoplay off, devices in shared spaces for younger children.

Contact. Who might reach them. Adults posing as children, or simply adults with too much access. The response is settings that limit who can message, and a child who tells you when someone new appears.

Conduct. What they do themselves and what other children do to them. Group chats, exclusion, pile-ons, sending things they cannot take back. The response is almost entirely conversation, because no setting addresses it.

Commerce. The part most often left out. In-game purchases, loot boxes, influencers selling things, and data collected about a child. The response is a payment method they cannot reach and a running conversation about who is making money here.

What to set up

Do this once, properly, and revisit twice a year.

  • Child accounts rather than adult ones, on every platform and device
  • Restricted or kids modes where they exist, autoplay off
  • Message settings limited to known contacts
  • No stored payment method on a child's device
  • Devices charging outside bedrooms overnight, adults included
  • Location sharing off in apps other than the ones you chose deliberately

None of this is a solution and all of it reduces the surface area. Treat it as the equivalent of a stair gate: useful at one age, quietly irrelevant later.

What to talk about

More useful than the settings, and the part that keeps working.

Watch things together sometimes, especially with younger children, and ask what they think rather than telling them. Ask who made this and why. Ask what happens if you scroll for an hour, and how you feel afterwards. Talk about specific situations before they arise: what would you do if somebody sent you something horrible, or asked for a photograph, or said not to tell me.

The one thing that matters most

Whether your child would tell you when something goes wrong. Everything else is secondary to that, and it is decided by what happens the first time they bring you something small.

Say it explicitly and in advance: if anything happens online that worries you, I will help first, and I will not take your phone away as the immediate response. Then honour it. A parent who confiscates on the first disclosure will not receive a second one.

By age, roughly

Under seven: shared spaces, chosen content, no open platforms. Design does the work.

Seven to eleven: child accounts, limited contact, watching together, the first real conversations.

Eleven to fourteen: more access, more conversation, settings agreed rather than imposed. Their social life is now partly here and treating that as trivial ends the conversation.

Fourteen and up: you are an adviser. Judgement, not restriction, is what is left, and it is what you have been building.

If you are worried about a specific situation, contact your local child protection service or a specialist online safety helpline.
cyber-safety-for-kids:
This is the practical, technical half of online safety: the habits worth building before they are needed rather than after. None of it requires expertise, and most of it is a single evening of setup plus a few conversations.

Passwords

The rule children are usually given is complexity. The rule that matters more is that passwords are not reused, because the common way an account is lost is not guessing but a leak somewhere else.

Three unrelated words are easier for a child to remember and harder to break than a short scramble of symbols. A password manager, including the one built into the browser, is a reasonable thing to set up together at around eleven.

And the social rule: passwords are not shared with friends, however close. This one needs saying explicitly, because sharing a password reads as an act of trust at twelve.

Two-factor authentication

Turn it on for their email, because whoever controls the email can reset everything else. This is the highest-value fifteen minutes in this whole article.

Recognising a scam

Children are targeted with the same tricks as adults, dressed differently: free game currency, a giveaway, an account upgrade, a message from a friend whose account has been taken. The common feature is urgency plus a link.

Teach one habit rather than a list: if a message wants you to hurry, stop. Check with the person another way. Nothing legitimate expires in four minutes.

The trail

Worth explaining honestly rather than as a warning. Things posted can be screenshotted, kept and resurfaced, including in apps that promise otherwise. Accounts set to private are private from the public, not from the platform or from a friend who takes a photograph of the screen.

The useful question, and it works better than any rule: would you be comfortable if this were still around in five years.

Public wifi and devices

Do not log in to anything that matters on shared or public wifi. Log out of accounts on borrowed devices. Lock the phone with a code that is not their birthday.

What to do when something goes wrong

Have this conversation before it does. Do not delete anything, because it may be evidence. Screenshot it. Block and report. Tell an adult. And from your side: help first, consequences later if at all.

Children hide problems mainly because they expect to lose the device. If the predictable outcome of telling you is losing the thing their friendships live in, they will take their chances alone.

The setup evening

Do it together rather than to them, at around ten or eleven. Strong distinct passwords on the accounts that matter, two-factor on the email, privacy settings reviewed, location sharing off except where deliberate, payment methods removed. A child who helped configure it understands it, and is far likelier to tell you when something changes.

If you are worried about a specific situation, contact your local child protection service or a specialist online safety helpline.
how-to-keep-children-safe-in-online-game:
Games are where most children meet strangers online. Not social media, which is the usual focus, but the voice chat in a game they have been playing happily for two years.

Why games specifically

Four features combine in a way few other places do. There is open voice or text chat with people who are not friends. There is a shared activity that builds rapport quickly, which is exactly how a relationship is formed. There is often a way to send items or currency, which creates obligation. And parents tend to see gaming as the safer option, so it is supervised less than social media.

That combination is the reason safeguarding organisations report a large share of online grooming beginning in games.

The settings that matter

Different in every game, and worth an hour once.

  • Voice and text chat: off, or restricted to friends only. This is the single biggest lever.
  • Who can send friend requests: nobody, or friends of friends.
  • Profile visibility: private. Usernames should not contain a real name, age or school.
  • Purchases: no stored card, password required, and check whether the console account has a balance.
  • Screen time and shutdown: where the platform offers it, because ending a game mid-match is what causes most of the conflict.

The conversations

People are not always who they say. Somebody claiming to be eleven may not be. Say it once, plainly, without making the game frightening.

Gifts create obligation. This is the one children do not anticipate. Free currency, a rare item, help levelling up. If somebody gives you something and then asks for something, come and tell me.

Never move to another app. A request to continue on a different platform, especially a private one, is the most common escalation step and is worth naming as a specific thing to report.

Nothing about you. No school, no area, no photographs, no daily routine.

You will not lose the game for telling me. Say it in advance and mean it.

Play it with them

More useful than any setting, and easier while they are young. Play the game occasionally, badly. Ask who they play with and how they know them. Let them explain the mechanics to you, which they will enjoy far more than being asked whether they are safe.

A parent who understands the game is a parent a child can describe a problem to without first explaining the whole world it happened in. That gap is a real reason children do not report.

The money question

Loot boxes and in-game currency are designed with the same mechanisms as gambling, and the resemblance is not accidental. Several countries have regulated them for that reason. Worth discussing openly rather than only blocking: what the odds are, why the currency is not priced in real money, and why the packs cost slightly more than the bundle you can buy.

If you are worried about a specific situation, contact your local child protection service or a specialist online safety helpline.
